United States: a Republican lawmaker files eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, mostly over the war with Iran, and a vote could come as soon as Wednesday

On Monday, November 9, Republican Thomas Massie filed eight articles of impeachment in the House against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, centered on the war with Iran waged without Congress's approval. A vote could take place by Wednesday, November 11, and Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries says he will vote in favor [1][2][3].
On Monday, November 9, Kentucky Republican Representative Thomas Massie filed eight articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth, directly on the floor of the House of Representatives [1][2].

The core of the charge is the war with Iran: three of the eight articles accuse Hegseth of violating Congress's war powers, and another accuses him of having "abused" his powers and "knowingly carried out" illegal orders [1][4].
The articles also cite the strikes on boats suspected of carrying drugs, which have killed at least 243 people; Massie also mentions the secretary's role in Venezuela and Yemen [4].

This type of resolution is called "privileged": Republican leadership must act within two legislative days. It can bring the text to a vote itself, move to bury it (a "motion to table") or refer it to committee, which Massie says would have the same effect [2][3].

Republicans hold only a 218-to-214 majority: it would take just three of them voting with all the Democrats to adopt the articles by simple majority. Removal itself would then require two-thirds of the Republican-controlled Senate [2][3].
Donald Trump said he would "back" Hegseth even if he were impeached; the secretary replied "we are not worried" and spoke of "fake impeachment articles" in a video posted on X [4][5].
The chair of the House Oversight Committee, Republican James Comer, refuses to support the procedure [7].

Key point: a lawmaker from the president's own party is forcing the vote, just days after the November 3 midterm elections, and is targeting the secretary in charge of running the war with Iran [1][3].

The procedure matters as much as the outcome. With a "privileged" resolution, a single lawmaker can force the House to take a position, and majority leaders can try to shelve the matter without a debate on the substance. According to Massie, House Speaker Johnson had already sent lawmakers home early in September to avoid this vote, and could repeat the maneuver this week [6][7].

Democrats are changing course. Hakeem Jeffries said on ABC that he would be a "firm yes" if the House votes, whereas in December 2025 he judged that Republicans would never let such articles reach the floor [2][5]. He blames Hegseth for being "the architect of the reckless, costly and failed war of choice in Iran" [4].

Massie is betting on defections: he considers it "very likely" that Hegseth will not end the year in office, and explains that lawmakers who lost their elections may feel freer to vote against him. No Republican has been named as committed to voting in favor [4][7].

Why it concerns you: the war with Iran is being fought around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a large share of the world's oil passes, so it affects the price of your tank of fuel and your energy bill. The U.S. Congress is one of the few brakes on the decision to continue this war: the vote on the secretary will show whether lawmakers from Donald Trump's camp are ready to contradict him, which could change the course of the conflict and of oil prices.

Brazil: Lula promises income tax exemption up to 5,000 reais and an end to the six-day work week, without saying how to pay for them, and the stock market rebounds 2.2%

On Sunday, November 8, in his first televised address since his re-election, Lula cited about a dozen priorities: no income tax up to 5,000 reais a month, an end to the six-day work week with no pay cut, and basic-basket taxes at zero from 2027. No cost or financing was given; the stock market gained 2.2% on Monday [1][2][3].

Lula addressed the nation on Sunday evening, November 8, on television for the first time since his re-election, and presented the priorities of his new term, about a dozen initiatives according to the Brazilian press [1][2][6].

The three clearest measures: exempting from income tax those who earn up to 5,000 reais a month, ending the "6x1" work schedule (six days worked for one day of rest) without cutting wages, and bringing taxes on basic-basket products down to zero from 2027 [1][2].
He also promised that the state will buy back household debts from banks and write off micro-entrepreneurs' debts owed to the Union, without giving the cost or the sources of financing [1][2][6].

On public finances, he said the debt trajectory and high interest rates worry him, promised to create the conditions for lower rates and to raise investment to 20% of GDP with the private sector; the Metrópoles columnist counted 42 seconds devoted to rates and debt [1][5][6].
He also urgently called for political and judicial reforms, with no text or timetable [10].
On Monday, November 9, the Ibovespa index gained 2.22% to 172,236 points according to most sources, driven by banks and Vale; the dollar stayed almost stable, around 5.50 reais [3][4].

This rebound owes a lot to the outside world: oil fell by nearly 6% after Donald Trump's statements on Iran and Wall Street rose [4]. Even so, the Ibovespa remains about 16% lower than before the election [9].
Key point: the speech reassures on tone ("fiscal responsibility") but gives neither figures nor a timetable, and that is what markets judge a government on [3][7].

The promises are expensive: exempting up to 5,000 reais or removing basic-basket taxes deprives the state of revenue, while debt is rising. According to Metrópoles, gross debt was at 71.68% of GDP in January 2023 and nominal debt rose from 7.2 trillion to 11.1 trillion reais [5]. Heavier debt pushes lenders to demand higher rates, which also makes the promised rate cuts harder.

Economists are divided but cautious. InfoMoney judges that the speech repeated campaign promises that in practice raise spending and prevent rate cuts, and one economist sees a risk of a crisis comparable to that of 2015 [7]. An analyst quoted by Money Times says Lula "is getting closer to the market with general phrases" [8].

The context sharpens the stakes: the Focus bulletin raised its projection for the Selic policy rate for 2026, which pushes back the idea of a quick cut, and Lula did not say who will head the Finance Ministry [3].

For you: Brazil is a major supplier of soybeans, coffee and iron ore. When its stock market or currency wobbles because investors doubt its public finances, prices and investments tied to emerging countries become more uncertain. A state that promises to cut taxes without saying how it will replace them exposes itself to higher borrowing rates: that is precisely what markets are watching here.
Coming weeks
Lula must still say who will head the Finance Ministry, and the cost and financing of the announced measures remain to be published [3][1].

Western Sahara: after 35 years, the UN winds down its MINURSO mission, a victim of a Russian veto, and the General Assembly debates it on Tuesday

On October 30, the Security Council adopted neither the U.S. draft, blocked by Russia, nor the Russian counter-draft: MINURSO's mandate expired, a first since 1991. Its liquidation began on November 1, and the UN General Assembly is due to debate it this Tuesday, November 10 [1][3][5][7].

On October 30, the Security Council voted on two texts on Western Sahara without adopting either: the U.S. draft extended the mission until October 31, 2027 and renamed it the "United Nations Mission for Western Sahara" from November 1; it received eleven votes in favor, one against (Russia) and three abstentions [4][5].

The Russian counter-draft, a simple renewal until October 31, 2027, gathered three votes in favor (China, Somalia, Russia), one vote against from a permanent member (the United States) and eleven abstentions; Washington explained that it could not support a mandate that had not met its objectives [5].
This is the first non-renewal of MINURSO's mandate since its creation in 1991: the mission, which had been extended in 2025 until October 31, 2026, has ceased operations [6][9].

On November 1, the UN made the start of the liquidation period official, entrusted to a reduced team, and the mission's 13 sites are to close; according to the Boutros-Ghali Observatory, this phase will take several months [3][6].

António Guterres insisted that MINURSO's departure "in no way calls into question" the "inalienable right to self-determination" of the people of Western Sahara, and asked all parties to cooperate so that the liquidation is "orderly" [1][2].

The General Assembly is due to debate the issue on Tuesday, November 10; according to RFI quoted by Qz, Russia will have to explain its veto there, and reactions from Morocco and Algeria are expected [7].

Key point: for the first time in 35 years, no UN peacekeeper is monitoring the ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front in Western Sahara, a territory the UN still classes as a non-self-governing territory [1][3][8].

The deadlock is a crossed veto. Washington wanted to relaunch the mission around Morocco's autonomy plan, which the U.S. text placed at the center of the settlement; Moscow considers this approach unbalanced and vetoed it; the United States then refused the simple renewal proposed by Russia [3][4][5].

Morocco is therefore looking for another arena: according to Médias24, it is taking the issue to the General Assembly's Fourth Committee, which approved a draft resolution on the Sahara on October 15 by 152 votes to 2 with 7 abstentions, a text that still has to be endorsed by the General Assembly [8].

The risk is one of security as much as diplomacy: Guterres warned of a possible resumption of hostilities, and analysts point to a risk of escalation between Morocco, the Polisario Front and Algeria, a country that had not voted for the last extension in 2025 [2][9][10]. The Moroccan sources, very present here, should be read with caution: some present the outcome as a victory for Rabat, others as a setback.

For you: Morocco is a close partner of France and Spain for trade, phosphates, cars and migration; Algeria is a gas supplier to Europe. A conflict heating up between these two neighbors, already on cold terms, can weigh on energy, migration routes and French companies based in the Maghreb. It is also a test for the UN: its oldest peace mission in North Africa is disappearing for lack of agreement among major powers.

Senegal: the Assembly rejects the amended budget and its Finance Committee rejects the 2027 budget, as Moody's says a debt exchange would "very likely" be a default

Senegal is sinking into budget deadlock: the Assembly rejected the amended 2026 budget on November 3, and the Finance Committee rejected the 2027 budget on November 7. Yet the $2.2 billion IMF deal depends on them, and Moody's, which cut the country's rating to Ca, speaks of default [1][2][3][4][5].

On November 3, the National Assembly rejected the amended 2026 finance bill, through a "previous question" motion by lawmaker Amadou Ba, with no debate on the substance; the published vote counts differ depending on the outlet [1][8].

The text raised the 2026 deficit forecast to 7.6% of GDP, from 5.4% previously, and cut planned investment by 555 billion CFA francs; lawmakers from Pastef, despite holding the majority, dispute the accuracy of the figures [2][8].

On November 7, the Finance Committee rejected the revenue forecasts and the public debt budget of the 2027 finance bill, which provides for 6,012.1 billion CFA francs in revenue against 7,363.7 billion in spending [3][6][9].
This deadlock threatens 480 billion CFA francs earmarked to pay the state's arrears to private companies [7].

Senegal is negotiating with the IMF a program of about $2.2 billion over three years (2026-2029): a staff-level agreement was reached in September, after audits that put debt at around 130% of GDP; it still has to be approved by the IMF's executive board [1][3][5].

On October 29, Moody's cut Senegal's foreign-currency rating from Caa2 to Ca and estimated losses for private external creditors at between 35% and 65%; on November 6, it warned that a bond exchange linked to the restructuring would "very likely" be a default, while noting that Dakar is still making its payments [4][5].
Markets are following: the yield on five-year bonds reached 8.24% at the last regional auction, and the eurobonds trade at around 50 to 52 cents on the dollar [2][5].
Key point: without a voted budget, the Senegalese state struggles to pay its expenses and to convince the IMF to release its program, while its debt puts it on the brink of default [1][3][5].

The conflict is first of all political. Lawmakers from Pastef, the ruling party, are blocking the budget presented by the government, in a standoff that has lasted since the dismissal of Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko at the end of May 2026, according to one outlet; Pastef's secretary general, Bocar Faye, claims the rejection was done at Sonko's wish, but the sources do not settle his current role [8].

The practical stakes are heavy. The finance minister warned of "very limited" room for maneuver and of difficulties in accessing financial markets; he considers that rejecting the amended budget does not require withdrawing the 2027 budget, whereas the chair of the Finance Committee judges that the latter's assumptions are called into question [1][3][6]. One site also suggests that legal tools would allow the head of state to bypass the deadlock [10].

For creditors, the equation is simple: restructuring debt means making lenders lose money, which rating agencies treat as a default. That is why Moody's cut the rating, while raising the outlook from negative to stable [4][5].

For you: Senegal is one of the West African countries most closely tied to France (trade, diaspora, French companies). A default or a lasting deadlock can make credit more expensive, delay payments to companies and weigh on jobs and on the money transfers of diaspora families. It is also a concrete example of what a "hidden debt" is: when the real figures come out, lenders change their minds.

Paraguay: new president Alliana asks all his ministers to resign, while prosecutors search Santiago Peña's house in the Ueno bank case

Paraguay is in the midst of a banking and political crisis: after the takeover of Ueno bank on November 3, which froze the money of nearly three million customers, President Santiago Peña fell. His successor Pedro Alliana is asking all his ministers to put their posts at his disposal, and prosecutors are targeting Peña [1][2][3].

On November 3, Paraguay's central bank took control of Ueno bank; its solvency ratio had fallen to less than half the legal minimum, and nearly three million people lost access to their money, which triggered protests [1].

Lawmakers voted to impeach President Santiago Peña, who submitted his resignation on November 5, pending his trial by the Senate; Pedro Alliana, his vice president, took over the presidency by constitutional succession [1][4][5].
On Monday, November 9, prosecutors searched Peña's house in Asunción and asked for the cooperation of the United States, Luxembourg and Argentina to trace funds diverted abroad [6].

Peña is accused of having used his influence to steer millions of public deposits to Ueno and of having played down the bank's difficulties despite warnings about doubtful loans; Democracy Now says he was placed under house arrest, other sources say pretrial detention, which remains to be confirmed [1][3].
On November 9, Alliana asked his ministers, secretaries and top officials of trust to submit their resignations, through his new chief of staff, Rolando de Barros [2][5].

He also proposed Jorge Schreiner to head the central bank, subject to Congress's approval; the former central bank chief, Carlos Carvallo, a former Ueno executive, resigned and faces criminal prosecution [1][2].
Key point: in one week, the failure of a bank brought down a president, and the country must now restore trust in its banking system and in its institutions [1][2].

The case shows what happens when the regulator and the bank blur together: the head of the central bank, Carlos Carvallo, himself came from Ueno [1]. When a bank is judged insolvent, the central bank takes it over and freezes accounts while it works out who pays; protests broke out after the accounts were blocked [1].

Politically, Alliana's overhaul of the government aims to turn the page without waiting. But he himself was named in the case: the sources indicate that he is not being prosecuted and that Congress dropped the idea of impeaching him [5][6]. The investigation, which seeks to follow the money abroad, will show whether the crisis stops at Peña or extends to other officials [6].
For the economy, everything depends on what comes next: the appointment of the new central bank chief, how savers will be repaid and investors' confidence in the country [1][2].

For you: the case is a reminder that a bank failure is first of all a problem of trust, not just of money. In Europe, deposit guarantees exist precisely to prevent a panic of this kind from starting. In Paraguay, it is trust in the entire state that has been shaken, with possible effects on investment and credit in this country neighboring Brazil and Argentina.

news.2026-11-10-mexique-inflation-3-75-o: Mexico: inflation rises for the third month in a row, to 3.75% in October, its highest level since May, with tomatoes and electricity

The statistics institute INEGI published annual inflation of 3.75% for October on November 9, against 3.45% in September and 3.26% in August. Prices rose 0.65% over the month, driven by green tomatoes, air transport and the end of an electricity subsidy [1][2][3].
Mexican annual inflation went from 3.26% in August to 3.45% in September, then to 3.75% in October, the highest level since May; in October alone, prices rose 0.65% [1][2][3].
Core inflation, which sets aside the most volatile products such as fresh food and energy, rose 0.34% over the month and reached 3.80% over one year [3].
Green tomatoes and air transport led the increases; INEGI also cites the end of the summer electricity rate subsidy in 18 cities [1][2].
This rise comes as the central bank (Banxico) has brought its policy rate down to 6.25%, a level it should hold for an extended period according to a PorEsto headline [3].
Key point: Mexican inflation has been rising for three months and now exceeds 3.7%, just as the central bank has cut its policy rate to 6.25% [1][3].
With core inflation (3.80%) slightly above headline inflation (3.75%), the rise does not come only from tomatoes, whose price is very volatile: the movement also affects other prices [3].

For you: Mexico is a major trading partner of the United States and a supplier of parts for car factories; when its prices and rates change, the peso moves and so do production costs, which sometimes ends up in the price of cars or imported vegetables.

news.2026-11-10-colombie-loi-de-sauvetag: Colombia: President De la Espriella's "rescue law", with 45 to 51 trillion pesos of adjustment, must be voted in under six weeks

Filed on October 29, President Abelardo de la Espriella's economic rescue bill mixes spending cuts, a VAT increase and a corporate tax cut, from 35% to 31%. It does not yet have rapporteurs and Congress has less than six weeks to vote on it [1][2][3][4].
The text, filed on October 29, lowers corporate tax from 35% to 33% in 2027 then 31% from 2028; a Banco de Bogotá study puts its cost at 0.19% of GDP in 2027 and 0.42% in 2030 [1][2].

The presidency expects a public deficit of 144 trillion pesos at the end of 2026; the targeted adjustment varies by outlet, from 45 to 51 trillion pesos, of which nearly 70% would come from spending cuts [1][5].
According to El Colombiano, the reform changes VAT and health contributions, which contrasts with the campaign promise not to raise taxes; its opponents say it mainly benefits large corporations [4].

Former president Iván Duque backs the bill but warns that a budget crisis could be "chaotic"; El Tiempo notes that the government has less than six weeks before the end of Congress's ordinary session, with no rapporteurs appointed [3][6].
Key point: the government has to convince a hesitant Congress to vote both savings and tax increases before the end of the year, failing which the deficit stays out of control [3][5].
Banco de Bogotá reviewed the measures in the text most likely to be adopted in Congress: not all of them will pass, and the final adjustment figure will depend on those that are voted [2].

For you: Colombia is a supplier of oil, coal and coffee. A country that fails to put its accounts right risks seeing its borrowing rates rise and its currency fall, which affects its companies and its imports.

news.2026-11-10-australie-ia-regulateur-: Australia: Albanese announces an AI regulator and six mandatory guardrails, after the Medicare hacking affair involving OpenAI

On November 10, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the creation of an AI safety regulator, with "significant penalties", and six mandatory rules for companies. The government accepts all 18 recommendations of a review launched after an incident involving OpenAI [1][2][3][4].
The regulator will enforce six mandatory guardrails: security checks, risk management, prompt reporting of cybersecurity incidents and publication of safety frameworks [2][3].
The future laws will also pave the way for independent assessment of the AI models used by technology companies [2].

Albanese says his government accepted the 18 recommendations of the review of the incident and has begun implementing them; one calls for mandatory reporting, within a set deadline, of breaches or harm caused by AI [3][4].

According to the ABC, OpenAI broke no law in the Medicare-related hacking affair, which is pushing the government to fill a legal gap; the fines and the reporting deadline have not yet been published [1][4].
Key point: Australia is choosing to control AI companies through a law and a dedicated regulator, with penalties that could go as far as criminal ones according to the ABC [1][3].
The text of the law is still being drafted: the details (amount of fines, reporting deadline) will decide the real reach of the rules for large foreign AI labs [1][4].
For you: the European Union already has its AI regulation; Australia joins the countries imposing rules on the sector's giants, and global companies will have to adapt to several regimes at once.

news.2026-11-10-equateur-noboa-carburant: Ecuador: Noboa cuts fuel by five cents a gallon from November 12, 19 cents lower since July, but Super gasoline has risen

President Daniel Noboa announced on November 9 a cut of five cents of a dollar per gallon for Extra gasoline, Ecopaís and diesel, from November 12 to December 11. That makes 19 cents lower since July, under a band system that limits monthly changes [1][2][3].
Extra and Ecopaís go from 3.17 to 3.12 dollars a gallon and diesel from 3.11 to 3.06 dollars; Vistazo gives 3.16 for the old gasoline price, hence a small gap between sources [1][2].
The new prices apply from November 12 to December 11; according to Noboa, the cumulative cut reaches 19 cents since July [1][2].
Since July 9, prices have been revised monthly under a band system: at most +5% or −10% compared with the previous month; these fuels are no longer subsidized, according to the EFE agency [1].
Super gasoline, for its part, rose in October, from 4.89 to 5.42 dollars a gallon, according to Teleamazonas [4].

Key point: the cut comes in the middle of the war in the Middle East, which the EFE agency cites as a factor in fuel costs worldwide [1]. Ecuador no longer subsidizes these fuels: the price follows a band mechanism revised monthly [1].

The country has one of the lowest gasoline prices on the continent: El Universo ranks it third cheapest in Latin America and the Caribbean [3]. But Super gasoline, outside the scheme, climbed in October [4].

For you: even a distant country like Ecuador is affected by what happens in the Gulf. Its system of monthly bands shows another way of smoothing fuel price shocks than subsidies or state stocks, as in France.
